new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened. The §1.3 Stress passage is at excerpt lines 67-84 (header '348 THE GRAMMAR SKETCHES' at line 64, i.e. p. The prose sentence is there verbatim: 'Words of two syllables have stress on the first; words of three or more syllables have primary stress on the second and, where relevant, secondary stress on every second syllable after that:'. Minor differences only: the scanned lays the three examples out column-wise (/nodi/ /e-nodi/ /nodi-nodi/ then ['nodi] [e'nodi] [no'dino.di] then the glosses 'cough' / 'he coughs' / 'cough (present)'); the reader's quote reassembles them row-wise, and the scanned renders the secondary-stress mark as '.', as the reader flagged. No other stress or accent…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the second syllable of the word in words of three or more syllables; in disyllabic words it falls on the first syllable (so stress is never word-final). Secondary stress falls on every second syllable after the primary (a binary rhythm counted from the left after the initial unstressed syllable), e.g. /nodi-nodi/ [no'dino,di]. A fixed: penultimate syllable reading fails for four-syllable words ([no'dino,di] has primary on the second, not the penult), so fixed: second syllable with a disyllable exception is the best label.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: 'where relevant, secondary stress on every second syllable after that' (i.e. on the fourth, sixth.. syllables after the primary on the second).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables are the stated exception to second-syllable stress: they take initial stress (i.e. final stress is avoided). No lexical exceptions mentioned.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'Words of two syllables.. words of three or more syllables'; examples are single phonological words including a prefixed verb form (/e-nodi/) and a reduplicated form (/nodi-nodi/), so affixed words count as the stress domain. No statement about phrase-level stress or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Ross 2002 describes 'the dialect.. spoken in the coastal village of 'Ala'ala' of the language 'variously referred to in the literature as Lala, Nara or Pokau' (= Glottolog lala1268, ISO nrz), with additional data from a speaker of Oloi (Bada'ai) village; Clunn & Kolia 1977 cover the Vanumae dialect. No separate dialect glottocodes are involved.

sources.note: §1.3 Stress (p. 348): disyllables stressed on the first syllable; words of three or more syllables have primary stress on the second syllable and secondary stress on every second syllable after that; examples ['nodi], [e'nodi], [no'dino.di]. Sketch adapted from Symonds 1989 plus Ross's own fieldnotes (speaker from Oloi/Bada'ai village); dialect of 'Ala'ala village.
WALS lists Clunn & Kolia 1977 and Lanyon-Orgill as sources for Lala but has no values for the stress features (14 Fixed Stress, 15 weight-sensitive Stress, 16 Weight Factors, 17 Rhythm Types).
